title: Work items and the management page: how to finish them

steps.path: The cards/ folder, and the management page's bulk edit
steps.headline: Where should changes to the work items be saved?
steps.today: The 144 work items live on this session's branch. The page saves each bulk edit (Combine, Move to stage, Delete) to whatever branch the copy it runs from is on, then commits and pushes.
steps.problem: After merging, the only copy on master is the shared folder, and it refuses all commits by design, so bulk edit would fail with 'commit failed'. And while chats edit items on their own branches, each one sees a different list until it merges: two chats can move the same item two ways, and the page shows only one of them.
steps.proposal: Pick where item changes are saved. This decides whether the page and every chat always see the same list.

options.label: Straight to master
options.summary: One dedicated copy of master saves item changes and pushes them at once, without a pull request. The page and every chat save through it.
pros: The page and every chat see the same list within seconds.
Item changes never clash when a branch merges.
Bulk edit keeps working after merge.
cons: Item edits skip the pull request step (they are bookkeeping, not app code).
A wrong bulk Delete lands on master at once; it can be undone from history, but not by a button yet.

options.label: On each chat's branch
options.summary: As now: an item change rides along with that chat's work and reaches master when it merges.
pros: Item changes are reviewed with the work they belong to.
cons: The page shows a stale or partial list.
Two chats editing the same item clash at merge.
Bulk edit fails when run from master; it only works from a chat's copy.

options.label: A file outside git
options.summary: Items live in a plain folder on this computer, not in any repo.
pros: Instant, nothing to commit or push.
cons: No history: a bad edit cannot be undone.
Not backed up, and your other computer never sees them.

steps.headline: Should the foundation merge soon, with the rest built afterwards on new branches?
steps.today: Nothing is merged. Master has moved on 34 commits, changing the old roadmap files three times; this branch deletes those files. 14 other branches also edit the old roadmap, mostly old and idle. Trial merge: 3 old-roadmap clashes plus 1 clash in a check rule, all small.
steps.problem: Every day unmerged, chats on master keep writing to the old roadmap, and each of those entries must be moved into items again by hand. When an old branch later merges, it would quietly bring the old roadmap files back.

options.label: Merge the foundation soon
options.summary: Bring master's changes in, turn its 2 new roadmap edits into items, fix the clashing check, add a check that refuses old-roadmap files coming back, verify, then ask you 'ready to merge?'. Buttons, chat recording and cleanup follow on new branches.
pros: Clashes stop growing; every chat starts filing items instead of roadmap entries.
Each later piece is a small, separate merge you can judge on its own.
cons: Until the later pieces land, the page still has 'not built yet' buttons and Oct 12 snapshot sections. Only you see the page.

options.label: Finish everything first
options.summary: Build the buttons, chat recording and cleanup on this branch, then merge once.
pros: One merge, and the page is complete the day it lands.
cons: Clashes grow daily; roadmap entries written meanwhile must be moved again.
A very large merge is harder to check and harder to undo.

steps.intro: Seven buttons on the page only say 'not built yet'. These two questions decide how they get built.

steps.headline: Should the management page become a page inside the YouCoded app?
steps.today: The page is a browser tab that exists only while a chat runs 'node manage.mjs'. Separately, since Oct 14, YouCoded Pages (small apps inside YouCoded) can open the normal new-chat window with a message already filled in; you still pick the project and press Start.
steps.problem: A browser tab cannot start, resume or switch to a chat in the app, so 'Start a chat on this', 'Resume latest chat' and 'Go to chat' have nothing to call. And the page vanishes when its chat ends.
steps.proposal: Two homes for the page. Not yet checked: whether a Page can already save files (needed for bulk edit) and open a specific older chat; both may need a small new app ability, tested in a dev window, never your installed app.

options.label: A page inside the app
options.summary: The management page becomes a YouCoded Page, always one click away in the app.
pros: Always available, no chat needed to run it.
'Start a chat on this' uses the ability that shipped Oct 14.
Follows your app theme automatically.
cons: App changes; your installed app only gets them with the next release.
Resume and Go to chat probably need a new Page ability first.
Desktop only at first; the phone app has no Pages yet.

options.label: Stay a browser tab
options.summary: Buttons copy a ready-made message (for example 'Resume item #75') that you paste into a chat.
pros: Small and quick; no app changes or release needed.
cons: You paste every time.
The page still needs a chat running to exist.

steps.path: The 'Merge to master' button on an item
steps.headline: What should 'Merge to master' actually do when pressed?
steps.today: The button shows on an item whose pull request passes its checks, and only says 'not built yet'. A real merge here means: merge, push, run the close-out checks, archive the item's plan documents, mark the item Merged, and remove its copies and branches.
steps.problem: Done half-way (merged but not cleaned up), it leaves stale copies of work and an item still showing as unfinished.
steps.proposal: Two ways the button could work.

options.label: Opens a chat that merges
options.summary: Opens the new-chat window with 'Merge item #75 to master' filled in; you press Start and the chat does every step and reports back.
pros: Every step runs, with the same checks as when you ask in chat.
If something fails, the chat explains it and can fix it.
cons: One extra click (Start), and about a minute instead of seconds.

options.label: The page merges itself
options.summary: The page merges the pull request directly, after a 'Merge to master?' confirmation.
pros: One click, seconds.
cons: Cleanup and checks would be rebuilt in the page, a second copy that can drift.
A failure mid-way leaves a half-done state with no chat to explain it.

steps.intro: The page is only as good as its facts. These decide how items stay accurate.

steps.path: The start and end of every work chat
steps.headline: Should every work chat join an item at its start and close it automatically at merge?
steps.today: Chats don't record themselves on items. Only 11 of 144 items are linked to any branch, by hand. 'cards.mjs close' marks an item Merged but is run by hand. The 'Working' marker is a guess: any linked branch with a commit in the last 24 hours shows as Working, though you decided Working comes only from a live signal.
steps.problem: 'Several chats on one item' can't be tracked if chats don't say which item they're on, and an item stays unfinished after its work merges unless someone remembers.
steps.proposal: Yes: at its start, a work chat finds the matching item (or proposes a new one the idea-intake way and waits for your yes), names its branch after it (for example 75-project-skills), and records itself on it; merging moves the item to Merged on its own; 'Working' shows only while a chat is actually open on it. No: items stay hand-linked and the Working guess stays.

steps.path: The 143 items moved over from the old roadmap
steps.headline: How should the moved-over items be sorted into their real stages?
steps.today: 113 items sit in Planning, 28 in Preliminary exploration, 2 in Agentic buildout, 1 in Human polish & review. None has a finish line (the 1 to 3 sentences saying when it's done), which the plan said each would carry.
steps.problem: You defined Planning as 'thought through, no overlaps', but the move put almost the whole old roadmap there. Some of it is loose ideas, some is probably already done in merged work, and some overlaps.

options.label: Proposals in batches
options.summary: I check each item against merged history and the others, then show you batches of about 20 on a deck: back to Exploration, already done (Merged, with what shipped it), or combine. You approve each batch.
pros: Nothing moves without your yes.
Each batch is small enough to judge.
cons: About 6 decks of your time.

options.label: I sort, you check
options.summary: I move them all, with a note on each, and you review with the page's bulk edit afterwards.
pros: Fastest for you up front.
cons: Changes you didn't approve: you'd have to find what moved and why.

options.label: Leave as is
options.summary: Sort each item only when a chat starts work on it.
pros: No time spent now.
cons: Planning stays crowded and partly wrong, so the page overstates what's ready.

steps.path: The Screens, Big picture and Tidy up sections, and the 'Facts as of Oct 12' header
steps.headline: What should happen to the sections still showing the Oct 12 snapshot?
steps.today: Today is live from the items. Screens, Big picture and Tidy up still show a copy made Oct 12, and the header says 'Facts as of Oct 12' for the whole page. Item #147 already covers redoing Screens.
steps.problem: A page that mixes live and three-day-old facts, with one date in the header, can't be trusted at a glance.
steps.proposal: Two ways to handle it until #147.

options.label: Make two live now
options.summary: Big picture reads the items directly (it was designed from the same facts); Tidy up reads the idle copies of work live. Screens keeps its pictures with its own 'Pictures from Oct 12' date, until #147. The header date goes.
pros: Everything except Screens is current every time you open it.
cons: More work before the page is done.

options.label: Label them, wait for #147
options.summary: Each snapshot section gets its own 'as of Oct 12' line; nothing else changes.
pros: Quick and honest.
cons: Big picture and Tidy up drift further out of date each day.

steps.surface: Copies of work on this computer
steps.headline: What should happen to the 9 copies of work idle 2+ weeks and never merged?
steps.today: 9 folders (model picker tags, per-project skills, specialists plans x3, theme plugin update, usage visibility, two old plan comparisons) were last touched Sept 11 to Sept 29. All have unsaved changes, and most hold work never merged.
steps.problem: They take space and show up as unfinished work, but some may hold the only copy of something you'd want.

options.label: Decide one by one
options.summary: A deck with one row per copy: what it was, what's unsaved, which item it belongs to. You pick keep or clean for each; clean means back up every change to GitHub first, then remove the folder.
pros: Nothing is lost by accident.
cons: One more deck.

options.label: Back up and clean all
options.summary: Every unsaved change is pushed to GitHub on its branch, then all 9 folders are removed.
pros: Done in one step; the work stays on GitHub.
cons: Old half-done changes get pushed as-is, without anyone looking.

options.label: Keep them all
options.summary: Leave them; the start-of-chat warning keeps listing them.
pros: No risk.
cons: The warning keeps appearing every chat.
